 Staying up late at weekends may increase the risk of suffering a stroke , research has suggested.
 Experts looking at the impact of sleep on the heart found that varying bedtimes and changing durations of sleep could have a harmful effect.
 Researchers from Harvard Medical School analysed data from more than 10,000 adults over a period of more than one million nights of sleep.
 They looked at sleep data from activity tracking devices and analysed participants’ sleep quantity, sleep quality, and how much of the night a person spent awake after first falling asleep.
 Researchers analysed whether sleep duration, bedtime and wake-up time changed from night to night over around six months, as well as the usual times a person fell asleep and woke up.
 Changes in schedule linked to risk
 They also looked at the number of sleep cycles each night, which is when a person moves from the end of the rapid eye movement (REM) stage, through light and deep sleep and back to REM, as well as people’s natural tendencies to be a night owl or an early bird.
 The results showed that changes in a person’s sleep schedule from night to night over around six months were linked to a 20 to 23 per cent higher risk of serious issues, including heart attack, stroke and heart failure.
 These risks increased with every 29-minute difference in sleep from night to night, including a 29 per cent higher risk of heart muscle disease, which can stop the heart effectively pumping blood through the body, and a 20 per cent higher risk of heart failure.
 Meanwhile, people who had a greater number of complete sleep cycles each night were linked to a 28 per cent lower risk of atrial arrhythmia, a common type of irregular heartbeat.
 But those with an unusually long sleep cycle were linked to a 55 per cent higher risk of heart attack or stroke.

 The research, which has yet to be peer reviewed, is being presented at the American Heart Association’s Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago.
 Dr Nguyen Minh Tuan Viet, the lead researcher and a neuroscientist from Boston Children’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School in the US, said: “While we often focus on getting a full eight hours of sleep every night, having a regular sleep schedule – consistent bedtimes, wake times, and sleep duration from night to night – is a practical, actionable step anyone can take that may help protect their heart and blood vessels.
  “Sleep irregularity is often due to weekends – we get to sleep a little bit later on a Friday night, or people have shift work. This may not be good for your heart health. 
 “Sometimes, the quality of sleep is something we cannot control. But the regularity, consistent bedtimes throughout the week and waking up at the same time every morning, is something some people can control.”
 People in the study had an average age of 53, and about seven in 10 were women. None had heart or metabolic disease at the start of the study.
 Sleep was tracked for around six months, and then people were followed for almost four years to see whether they suffered heart issues.
